meta.provenance: Generated from research/science-technology-graph by scripts/import-lifecycle.ts. Do not edit by hand.

events.label: by 3 October 1977
events.statement: Sanger, Nicklen and Coulson generated base-specific terminated extension products using nucleotide analogues and read the size-separated products on gels.
events.uncertainty: The paper used both dideoxy and arabino analogues and credited earlier inhibitor chemistry; it is not credited with the first φX174 genome report.

events.statement: A published research account described chain-termination dna sequencing.
events.uncertainty: This is a dated publication, not proof of first awareness, acceptance, external deployment or sale.

events.label: by Nov 1978
events.statement: Hamlyn and colleagues used an adaptation of the Sanger–Nicklen–Coulson method to sequence an immunoglobulin cDNA.
events.uncertainty: The 1978 work adapted the method for cDNA and shares the Cambridge MRC laboratory setting with the originating team; it is not proof of identical reagents, first outside use, or an independent institution.

events.label: Oct 2000
events.statement: The public consortium’s assembled draft provided broad human genome sequence coverage while retaining gaps and ambiguities.
events.uncertainty: Not a gapless genome, an inventory of every human variant, or proof that all reported gene-count interpretations remained correct.

events.label: by 6 July 2000
events.statement: UCSC reported that its public-consortium working-draft human-genome assembly had been posted on the web by 6 July 2000.
events.uncertainty: The original UCSC press release says the draft was already posted on 6 July; the later UCSC project history dates the web release to 7 July. This is not a resolved exact first-access date. The July draft predates and differs from the version assembled from data available on 7 October 2000.

events.statement: The public consortium published its analysis of a draft based on map and sequence data available on 7 October 2000.
events.uncertainty: The report does not establish the first public access to this exact assembled version or universal acceptance; some underlying data were released earlier.

events.statement: The public consortium sequenced mapped BAC/PAC clones with automated fluorescent reads and computational assembly.
events.uncertainty: This node is the public consortium configuration, not Celera’s whole-genome strategy or every possible way to assemble a genome.

events.statement: The international public human-genome effort moved its mapped-clone sequencing strategy into full-scale production.
events.uncertainty: Pilot activity occurred before this date; it is not asserted as the first use or a commercial offer.

events.statement: A published research account described mapped-clone genome sequencing.
events.uncertainty: This is a dated publication, not proof of first awareness, acceptance, external deployment or sale.

events.label: by 1974
events.statement: Sanger and Coulson used primed DNA synthesis, limiting nucleotide conditions, E. coli and T4 polymerases, and gel separation to infer sequences.
events.uncertainty: Not the first DNA sequencing attempt; earlier primed sequencing and synthetic-primer work are explicitly mentioned by the paper and remain backlog.

events.statement: A published research account described plus/minus dna sequencing.
events.uncertainty: This is a dated publication, not proof of first awareness, acceptance, external deployment or sale.

events.label: by 1977-2-24
events.statement: Sanger and collaborators used the plus/minus method to determine the φX174 sequence reported in Nature.
events.uncertainty: The application involved the originating team and collaborators; it does not establish an independent laboratory’s first use or a first commercial date.

events.label: c. 1890
events.statement: A granular metallic-contact device whose conductivity changes under electrical disturbance; this filings device is the predecessor Marconi calls a Branly coherer.
events.uncertainty: The 1890 original paper has not yet been inspected; museum retrospective dating is the present boundary. The 1900–1910 tripod object is not represented here, and Branly is not credited with the later complete communication system.

events.statement: Lodge describes and uses a metallic-filings receiver while demonstrating wireless signals.
events.uncertainty: Tube geometry and receiver details vary; this is not the later tripod commercial product.

events.statement: Faggin and Klein brought polysilicon-gate processing to ICs; Faggin redesigned an eight-channel analog multiplexer as the Fairchild 3708.
events.uncertainty: Not the origin of every self-aligned-gate idea: Bell Labs and Watkins antecedents are acknowledged as next-depth gaps.

events.label: by 1968
events.statement: Faggin recalled that the silicon-gate 3708 was being sold by the end of 1968.
events.uncertainty: Participant recollection; first sale, quantity and geography of customers unresolved.

events.statement: A battery-fed wire maintains contact through mercury while moving continuously around a magnetic pole; the following day’s arrangement improves wire and magnet support.
events.uncertainty: No claim of commercial usefulness or universal invention priority. The surviving 1822 object must not be used as an unqualified 1821 artifact.

events.statement: The Société Philomatique repeated Faraday’s wire-around-magnet experiment on 24 November 1821; Hachette separately acknowledged receiving an instrument from Faraday.
events.uncertainty: The letter does not unambiguously say the instrument Faraday sent was the instrument used in the repetition; mercury and exact mounting of the Paris apparatus are not independently specified.

events.label: 1 December 1957
events.statement: Hoerni proposed leaving oxide over the junction edges while opening contact areas, instead of stripping the oxide after diffusion.
events.uncertainty: The day is reported in a retrospective IEEE account; the original notebook itself was not inspected.

events.statement: Last team applied Hoerni planar processing to a working integrated flip-flop.
events.uncertainty: Use is specialist research use, not evidence of external commercial availability.

events.label: March 1959
events.statement: Hoerni demonstrated an early planar transistor prototype.
events.uncertainty: The unnamed working specimen is not established as a 2N1613; a 1962 patent publication does not date the working prototype.

events.label: October 1960
events.statement: Hoerni presented the planar transistor design and its characteristics at an electron-devices meeting.
events.uncertainty: The presentation describes the design, not proof that the particular 1959 prototype was shown or became the 2N1613.

events.label: by 1960-04
events.statement: Fairchild had sold the 2N1613, a planar silicon transistor of this general configuration, by April 1960.
events.uncertainty: The 1959 specimen’s polarity and identity are unproved; an April 1960 product sale does not establish the first commercial availability of the entire configuration class.

events.label: 15 November 1971
events.statement: On 15 November 1971 Intel advertised the MCS-4 family, including the 4004, as in stock for its merchant market.
events.uncertainty: The first day of merchant sales and possible earlier private merchant offers are unresolved. Earlier availability to Busicom under its contract is a different market scope.

events.label: January 1971
events.statement: A 4004 silicon run worked in January 1971; subsequent tests found and corrected minor errors.
events.uncertainty: The participants describe a working early iteration; this event is not a claim that it was the final mask sold in November.

events.label: Aug. 1895
events.statement: One oscillator terminal connects to earth and the other to an elevated conductor; the receiver similarly connects its coherer between earth and an elevated conductor. Telegraph key, relay and tapping receiver apparatus support signs.
events.uncertainty: 1895 configuration and date rely on a 1909 participant account. This node does not establish exclusive priority, universal obstacle penetration or the necessity of earth connection for all radio systems.

events.statement: Post Office engineers tested aerial-and-earth wireless telegraphy across the Bristol Channel.
events.uncertainty: The 1897 apparatus was a later implementation, not necessarily the original physical 1895 specimen.

events.statement: Noyce proposed deposited metal conductors crossing retained oxide to connect semiconductor regions without shorting junctions, including multi-device circuits.
events.uncertainty: No Kilby-to-Noyce transmission is claimed. This patent’s isolation configuration must not be silently equated with every later junction-isolated IC.

events.statement: Last team built a monolithic flip-flop based on the planar approach and Noyce interconnection patent.
events.uncertainty: May 1960 physical isolation cannot be equated to later junction-isolated sold products.

events.statement: A wire closing a galvanic circuit deflects a nearby suspended magnetic needle; moving the wire above/below reverses deflection; nonmagnetic needles provide controls.
events.uncertainty: The reported circular electrical-conflict explanation is historical. No claim that all magnetic phenomena or modern field theory were established in this experiment.

events.statement: De la Rive independently repeated Oersted current and needle experiment in Geneva.
events.uncertainty: The Geneva source reports the wire/compass effect, not the full set of original controls; its exact day is not specified beyond 1820.

events.statement: Frosch and Derick used silicon dioxide to protect wafers and delimit dopant diffusion through etched openings.
events.uncertainty: Masking depends on dopant and process conditions; no absolute impermeability to every dopant is asserted.

events.statement: Andrus and Bond adapted oxide masking to patterned photoengraved diffusion windows.
events.uncertainty: This is specialist research use; do not infer sales or exact later transfers.

events.statement: Jules Andrus and Walter Bond adapted photoresist patterning to etch windows in silicon oxide before localized diffusion.
events.uncertainty: This node is not Fairchild’s later step-and-repeat camera or DOFL’s separate diode-array work.

events.label: by 1958
events.statement: Fairchild used photolithographic oxide-window fabrication in its mesa transistor work and shipped 100 2N696 transistors by 1958.
events.uncertainty: The Fairchild method is contextual evidence of use of the same general patterned oxide-window process; the source does not identify every original Bell mask or prove exact transfer of a physical tool.

events.statement: Andrus issued patent publicly described photoresist-patterned windows in silicon oxide for selective diffusion.
events.uncertainty: A 1958 book chapter is cited by CHM but its text has not been inspected; patent is a later awareness bound.

events.statement: Repeated silver–zinc pairs with saline-wetted separators in a column; an explicitly described alternative connected dissimilar-metal bows through a chain of liquid-filled cups.
events.uncertainty: The accessed source is the Royal Society’s 1832 abstract, not the full 1800 French paper. Earlier construction dates and the later trough-battery design genealogy remain outside this node.

events.statement: Nicholson and Carlisle used a reproduced Volta pile in water-decomposition experiments in 1800.
events.uncertainty: The independent use is established for the stacked-pile arrangement; it does not establish use of the separate cups configuration or any first offer for sale.

events.label: April 1960
events.statement: Fairchild sold the 2N1613 planar transistor in April 1960.
events.uncertainty: The exact first-sale day and a fully exhaustive search of earlier offers remain open. Actual purchaser geography is not established by the inspected sources.

events.label: March 1961
events.statement: The Micrologic flip-flop was being sold in evaluation quantities in March 1961; the introductory unit price was $120.
events.uncertainty: The first day of the offer and the early samples isolation process are unconfirmed; five other elements were not yet generally available according to the March 31 report. Actual purchaser geography is not established by the inspected sources.

events.label: 50–120 CE
events.statement: Southern spring-fed aqueduct branch supplying Arelate before diversion to Barbegal.
events.uncertainty: Chronology is inherited archaeological synthesis; the branch is not the whole Arelate water system.

events.label: c. 120–130 CE
events.statement: Two rows of eight watermills supplied by the redirected southern aqueduct branch.
events.uncertainty: Wooden wheels are lost. Exact housing, output and customer reconstructions are outside this node.

events.label: by 300 CE
events.statement: The mill complex operated for years after the aqueduct was diverted and before its early-third-century abandonment.
events.uncertainty: The early-third-century dating is an inherited archaeological interpretation, not a precise date measured from the carbonate; the first operational day and customers are unknown.

events.label: 2800–2500 BCE
events.statement: Reservoirs east, south and west of the Castle, constructed during the Stage III urban expansion.
events.uncertainty: The interval dates a construction phase; it does not establish the exact age of every drain or later repair.

events.label: by c. 2500 BCE (inferred)
events.statement: The reservoirs were constructed as components of Stage III Dholavira’s urban water-management system, suggesting community water storage during that phase.
events.uncertainty: Use during the approximate construction phase is a contextual archaeological inference, not a directly dated operation. The upper bound is approximate, not a hard radiometric limit; access and exact commissioning are unknown.

events.statement: Seven woodblock-printed paper sheets joined into a scroll; the custodian identifies hemp and mulberry paper.
events.uncertainty: A surviving dated copy, not the invention of printing or paper. Findspot does not fix the printing workshop.

events.label: by 868 (inferred)
events.statement: A woodblock-printed scroll bearing an 868 colophon was made for universal distribution of the Buddhist text.
events.uncertainty: The colophon documents a distribution intention, not actual delivery to recipients. The custodian source was inspected online but a local cache could not be captured due to HTTP 403.

events.label: 8 March 1975
events.statement: Hōkūleʻa was launched on 8 March 1975 at Hakipuʻu-Kualoa, Kāneʻohe Bay, Oʻahu.
events.uncertainty: Launch proves the canoe had been built by this date but does not identify its exact construction-completion date or the first research voyage.

events.label: Built by 8 March 1975
events.statement: Hōkūleʻa had been built by its launch on 8 March 1975.
events.uncertainty: The completion date of construction is not specified; launch does not by itself establish practical research deployment.

events.label: April 1975
events.statement: The crew trained on Hōkūleʻa on Hawaiian waters in April 1975.
events.uncertainty: The photograph captions give April but not an exact day or first training sail. The 1976 interview is retrospective and does not itself date a particular practice; the distinct 1 May 1976 research voyage and 1975 swamping remain separate.

events.label: 1 May 1976
events.statement: The PVS canoe departed on its Hawaiʻi–Tahiti research voyage, guided by Mau Piailug using non-instrument wayfinding.
events.uncertainty: Practice voyages occurred before 1976 and modifications followed 1975 swamping; this anchor identifies the intended project voyage and does not claim first use of any kind. The contemporary article describes a planned escort; it does not independently establish the escort’s actual conduct.

events.statement: Kāne and Emory selected widely recorded canoe features as a hypothesis about earlier forms for an experimental vessel.
events.uncertainty: Widespread occurrence does not itself prove antiquity. The node records the investigators’ design inference, not its validation.

events.label: by 8 March 1975
events.statement: The project applied Kāne and Emory’s comparative design hypothesis in the construction of Hōkūleʻa by its 1975 launch.
events.uncertainty: The hypothesis was used for a named project; neither an exact first-use day nor general scholarly acceptance or accuracy is established.

events.statement: Surviving second volume of Jikji, printed using movable cast-metal characters.
events.uncertainty: No earliest-ever invention, exact alloy, casting procedure or China/Europe transfer claimed.

events.label: by 1377 (inferred)
events.statement: 1377 edition was printed for Zen teaching; its availability to that community is inferred.
events.uncertainty: No individual recipient or delivery date is established. The inference concerns Buddhist teaching community availability and does not prove sales or number of readers.

events.statement: Complete text of Jikji in a preserved woodblock edition.
events.uncertainty: Same text does not prove that the 1377 metal-type edition supplied the blocks or that one process caused the other.

events.label: by 1378 (inferred)
events.statement: 1378 edition was printed for Zen teaching; its availability to that community is inferred.
events.uncertainty: No individual recipient or delivery date is established. The inference concerns Buddhist teaching community availability and does not prove sales or number of readers.

events.statement: A pilot supplied at Malindi guided Vasco da Gama’s fleet across the Arabian Sea and interpreted coastal landmarks.
events.uncertainty: One narrated application; identity and religious labels are not adopted. No generic astrolabe, compass or Ibn Majid lineage is inferred.

events.statement: Datawell Directional Waverider G-4 deployments at navigator-selected wave patterns; GPS motion sensing produced directional spectra.
events.uncertainty: Exact campaign dates remain unresolved within the stated bounds; the survey is not a universal assessment of wavefinding.

events.statement: Mau Piailug guided Hōkūleʻa to Tahiti using noninstrument wayfinding.
events.uncertainty: 1976 dates this voyage, not the origin of Carolinian knowledge. No sweeping claim that all equipment aboard was nonmodern.

events.label: 1 May 1976
events.statement: Mau guided the Hōkūleʻa voyage toward Tahiti using noninstrument wayfinding after its 1 May 1976 departure.
events.uncertainty: This is the named voyage, not the origin of Satawal navigation or a claim that no substitute navigational approaches were possible.

events.statement: Mau taught Nainoa Thompson and collaborators to integrate wind, waves, swells, birds and stars in wayfinding.
events.uncertainty: This is a dated teaching episode, not the first creation or entirety of either community’s knowledge.

events.label: March–June 1980
events.statement: Thompson used learned wind, wave and celestial wayfinding cues during the 1980 Hōkūleʻa voyage, on which Mau also provided support.
events.uncertainty: Teaching and use are distinct; this does not prove full transfer of Mau’s knowledge or that the voyage was unaided.

events.label: by c. 4650 BCE
events.statement: Bifurcated channel F10 created by removal of basalt blocks; dated basal infill establishes an earlier excavated form.
events.uncertainty: Construction may be older. Charcoal association, old wood and stratigraphic interpretation limit precision; only F10 is represented.

events.label: by c. 1350 CE (inferred)
events.statement: Archaeological interpretation places initial use of F10 with its later walls within c. 1150–1350 CE.
events.uncertainty: This approximate archaeological interpretation is not a hard upper bound, a directly witnessed catch or proof of uninterrupted use since the much older basal infill. The source was inspected online; no local copy could be retained in the current pass.

events.label: c. 1150–1350
events.statement: Multi-tiered basalt walls added along the pre-existing F10 channel.
events.uncertainty: A long sedimentary hiatus separates phases; continuous operation or unchanged knowledge transmission is not established.

events.label: by c. 1350 CE (inferred)
events.statement: Archaeological interpretation places initial use of F10 with its later walls within c. 1150–1350 CE.
events.uncertainty: This approximate archaeological interpretation is not a hard upper bound, a directly witnessed catch or proof of uninterrupted use since the older channel. The source was inspected online; no local copy could be retained in the current pass.

events.label: by March 1980
events.statement: Thompson and Kyselka varied simulated latitude to study star rise/set positions and candidate latitude cues.
events.uncertainty: Display date is a by-date for the active method; earlier study duration is not narrowed. No claimed modern priority or accuracy distribution.

events.label: March–June 1980
events.statement: Thompson reported applying star-position cues studied in the planetarium to navigation during the 1980 voyage.
events.uncertainty: The article is a participant account; the precise first application and separate contribution of each cue are not documented.

events.label: by 537
events.statement: Hill mills powered by descending aqueduct water, operating before the siege’s supply cut.
events.uncertainty: Procopius says the mills were old; their original construction dates and complete number are not supplied.

events.label: 537 CE
events.statement: Procopius reports that mill machinery on moored boats operated in the Tiber to grind flour during the siege.
events.uncertainty: A literary report, not archaeological proof; exact day, number of mills, scale of flour supply and end of installation remain uncertain.

events.statement: Operating boat mills accompanied by an upstream iron-chain debris barrier and removal crew.
events.uncertainty: Procopius says protection against hostile boats was the stronger motive; this is not a milling-only device.

events.label: 537 CE
events.statement: The boat mills continued to operate with an upstream iron-chain barrier and a crew clearing intercepted debris.
events.uncertainty: The primary narrative is a participant’s retrospective account; the chain also protected against hostile boats and is not claimed to have had only one purpose.

events.label: 8 August 2018
events.statement: The test laboratory received a Glass Enterprise Edition 2 GG2 sample.
events.uncertainty: The report does not call this sample a prototype or specify when the model was invented or first built.

events.label: May 2019
events.statement: Google announced Glass Enterprise Edition 2 on 20 May 2019 and invited enterprise customers to contact its sales team or partners; a 21 May report described partner availability.
events.uncertainty: Google invited sales inquiries on 20 May; the independent availability report is dated 21 May. These do not establish the first transaction or exclude earlier private arrangements.

events.label: 4 February 2020
events.statement: On 4 February 2020 Google said developers and businesses could purchase Glass Enterprise Edition 2 devices directly from named hardware resellers.
events.uncertainty: Channel expansion, not the initial commercial introduction.

events.label: By 15 March 2023
events.statement: By 15 March 2023 Google was no longer selling Glass Enterprise Edition, including Edition 2; reseller withdrawal and last actual device use are not established.
events.uncertainty: No claim about last reseller sale, production, or actual installed-device use. Google says devices and existing software could continue after the support cutoff.

events.label: 15 September 2023
events.statement: Google identified a support and replacement cutoff for Glass Enterprise Edition.
events.uncertainty: A support cutoff is not a proven universal device end-of-use. Meet support may end while local device software remains usable.

events.statement: Eyepieces deliberately given a color-dependent magnification opposite to the remaining lateral color difference of the objective, so the combined microscope image has less color error away from the axis.
events.uncertainty: This specific compensation design is not a claim that eyepiece correction was wholly new. Compatibility depended on objective and eyepiece properties, not the name alone.

events.statement: By the 1889 catalogue, Zeiss listed compensating eyepieces at prices for different microscope bodies.
events.uncertainty: The 1886 date of being brought out and the 1889 price list do not establish the first sale or its day. The catalogue’s English and continental fittings identify instrument fit, not purchaser locations; distribution geography is not established.

events.statement: Thomas and Gilchrist modified the converter lining to remove phosphorus during Bessemer steelmaking.
events.uncertainty: Heritage account does not specify lining recipe or removal chemistry; those details are withheld.

events.label: by 1883
events.statement: By publication of the 1883 census survey, the basic-lined Thomas–Gilchrist process was reported in industrial use in Britain, France, Germany, Austria, Belgium and Russia.
events.uncertainty: The survey observes usage by publication, not its first date or universal adoption; the source gives no plant-by-plant audit.

events.label: c. 5000–4650 BCE
events.statement: Copper-bearing slag and slagged ceramic sherds document extraction of copper from ore at a Vinča settlement.
events.uncertainty: Small debris survives; convincing smelting installations were not identified. This node makes no sole-origin or universal-earliest claim.

events.label: by c. 4650 BCE
events.statement: Copper-bearing slag and slagged ceramics in the dated Belovode occupation imply local extractive smelting by the end of the cited horizon.
events.uncertainty: Small samples and contextual dating constrain a horizon; no specific first use, furnace form, economic exchange or global priority is established.

events.statement: Air blown through molten pig iron in a converter; oxidation supplies heat during conversion to steel.
events.uncertainty: The object page is retrospective. Its separate compressed statement about later improvements is not used.

events.label: by October 1858
events.statement: By October 1858 Göransson reported that his firm was using the Bessemer method in its works to make steel.
events.uncertainty: Contemporary self-report is preserved through a later Smithsonian history. It gives an upper bound, not the first sale, and does not prove all variations used identical equipment.

events.statement: Göran Fredrik Göransson applied the Bessemer method on a practical scale and obtained satisfactory steel ingots.
events.uncertainty: Institutional retrospective account; its universal-first and sweeping railway claims are not adopted.

events.label: by October 1858
events.statement: By October 1858 Göransson reported that his firm had shifted its works to steelmaking by the Bessemer process.
events.uncertainty: This is a retrospective transcription of a contemporary producer claim; exact commencement and buyer transactions remain unresolved.

events.statement: Faraday’s silicated borate of lead: a heavy optical glass finished and annealed in platinum trays after purification, mixing and fusion of the constituents.
events.uncertainty: The interval dates the reported development of this glass preparation; it does not establish the manufacture date of the particular specimen used in 1845, nor routine commercial optical performance.

events.label: by 6 November 1845
events.statement: By receipt of Faraday’s 1845 report, a piece of his heavy glass had been used as an optical medium in magnetic-rotation research.
events.uncertainty: This is a specialist research use, not evidence of marketed optical glass; the exact experiment day and the sample manufacture date remain unresolved.

events.label: by 1845
events.statement: Polarized light traversing Faraday’s heavy glass along a magnetic field changed its plane of polarization; reversing the magnetic poles reversed the rotation.
events.uncertainty: The material was his successful experimental medium, not a universal requirement for the effect; the paper also reports other substances and permanent magnets. This is distinct from mechanical electromagnetic rotation in 1821.

events.label: by 27 October 1864
events.statement: By 27 October 1864 Maxwell had used Faraday’s magnetic rotation as an observational indication in his field-theory argument.
events.uncertainty: This is a narrowly documented intellectual use by Maxwell; it is neither universal acceptance nor evidence that Faraday’s effect uniquely derived Maxwell’s theory. The physical location of Maxwell’s relevant work is not established by the inspected passage.

events.label: c. 3200 BCE
events.statement: Meteoritic iron hammered into sheet and rolled into tubular beads; a metalworking route requiring no extraction of iron from ore.
events.uncertainty: Three museum beads were directly analyzed. The manufacturing sequence is inferred from their structure; no transmission to later iron smelting is asserted.

events.label: by c. 3100 BCE
events.statement: Hammered and rolled meteoritic-iron beads formed part of the burial assemblages in Gerzeh during the dated Naqada horizon.
events.uncertainty: The beads were deposited in a broad dated horizon; deposition bounds an earlier manufacturing/use claim but does not fix its first date or show wider trade.

events.label: from c. 6550 BCE
events.statement: Large utilitarian tools forged from native copper; dated organic material remains embedded in some copper artifacts.
events.uncertainty: Associated organics date use indirectly. Sparse early finds and modeled cultural boundaries must not be equated; no claim of a global first.

events.label: c. 5570–4230 BCE, modeled onset (68% credible interval)
events.statement: The dated copper-bearing Old Copper sites and directly associated remains support local use of worked native copper in the modeled historical horizon.
events.uncertainty: Bebber et al. report a 68% credible interval for a modeled onset, so a real onset may lie outside either limit. Associations and individual artifact manufacture dates remain uncertain; the interval is not a known-by claim.

events.label: by 1886
events.statement: The Jena Glastechnisches Laboratorium supplied a wider selection of optical glasses, including borate and phosphate compositions with varied refractive-index and dispersion combinations.
events.uncertainty: No one universal composition is implied. Earlier prototypes and factory founding are not conflated with this availability endpoint; the exact glass or fluorite content of each objective remains unspecified.

events.statement: Zeiss reported that it used the new Jena glass in its microscope objectives from 1886.
events.uncertainty: The source establishes use in the Jena firm, not the first outside glass sale or the use of every specified glass formulation.

events.label: November 1952
events.statement: An operating LD plant converted carbon-rich hot metal into lower-carbon steel by oxygen blowing.
events.uncertainty: The 1966 judicial narrative reports November production; the operator dates commissioning to 27 November but does not establish the first heat on that day. No first sale or worldwide adoption is inferred.

events.label: 9th–early 10th c. CE
events.statement: Workshop crucibles interpreted as evidence for combining cast iron and wrought iron to produce steel.
events.uncertainty: Only the abstract was accessible in this pass; detailed context and competing metallurgical interpretations await full-text review.

events.label: by c. 1000 CE
events.statement: Workshop crucible remains at Merv indicate local crucible-steel production in the dated ninth–early tenth-century horizon.
events.uncertainty: Only the original abstract was accessible; co-fusion is an archaeological interpretation. The source says ninth–early tenth century and does not specify a numerical end; 1000 CE is a deliberately broad display bound, not a measured or certain date.

events.label: by c. 4650 BCE
events.statement: Tin-bronze foil interpreted as metal smelted from complex copper–tin ores, subsequently worked and annealed.
events.uncertainty: Ore identification is compositional inference. The broader group contains poorly contextualized finds; the node is restricted to the securely contextualized foil.

events.label: by c. 4650 BCE
events.statement: A worked tin-bronze foil was present in a Pločnik dwelling horizon by approximately 4650 BCE.
events.uncertainty: The context supplies a one-sided archaeological limit, not an exact date of manufacture, first alloying or a demonstrated common use; proposed vessel wrapping is tentative.

events.statement: Powell and Lealand made a 1/12-inch apochromatic objective to their own formula, with compensating eyepieces constructed on Abbe's plan; the combination was exhibited at the Society's November 1886 meeting.
events.uncertainty: The account says new glass samples reached English opticians but does not identify Powell and Lealand as recipients or establish which glass they used.

events.label: by 9 February 1887
events.statement: By his February 1887 address Dallinger had acquired another Powell–Lealand 1/12-inch apochromatic objective and expressed a strengthened favorable view.
events.uncertainty: One specialist’s acquisition and appraisal do not establish a sale, routine scientific use by others, or universal adoption.

events.label: 6th century CE
events.statement: A biography describes heating powdered cast iron with soft-iron blanks for several days to make steel for sabres.
events.uncertainty: Location and exact thermal procedure are uncertain. The modern label co-fusion does not establish that both components melted; the 1955 reconstruction is excluded.

events.label: by the end of the 6th century CE, reported
events.statement: The retrospective biography reports Qiwu producing sabres with a layered cast-iron and soft-iron treatment in a sixth-century military setting.
events.uncertainty: The passage is a later literary testimony, not surviving sixth-century workshop evidence; precise date, scale, technical interpretation and performance claims are uncertain.

events.statement: A dedicated experimental room and furnaces brought Faraday’s optical-glass experiments onto the Royal Institution premises, with Sergeant Anderson assisting.
events.uncertainty: This is a particular research installation, not the invention of a glass furnace. The entire manuscript was not inspected.

events.label: by 19 November 1829
events.statement: By Faraday’s 1829 lecture, the Royal Institution furnaces had been used continuously for the committee’s optical-glass experimental work.
events.uncertainty: The upper bound avoids claiming an exact first firing day; the use was for specialist research and does not imply a market or general industrial adoption.

events.statement: A manufactured series of microscope objectives using new glass materials and optical formulae, designed to improve chromatic and spherical correction and paired with compensating eyepieces.
events.uncertainty: Design and marketing claims are not treated as universal measured superiority. Dallinger’s later comparisons found limits; exact proprietary prescriptions are absent from these passages.

events.statement: By the 1889 catalogue, Zeiss offered several apochromatic objective sizes at stated prices.
events.uncertainty: The price list is an offer, not proof of a completed sale or the earliest offering; quoted performance advantages are manufacturer claims. The catalogue’s English and continental fittings identify instrument fit, not purchaser locations; distribution geography is not established.

events.label: 500–301 BCE
events.statement: CB3 combines a leaded-bronze head with the treated iron shaft.
events.uncertainty: Casting-on is proposed, not directly observed in manufacture.

events.label: by c. 301 BCE (museum attribution)
events.statement: A completed composite crossbow bolt with a bronze head and an iron shaft existed within the museum-attributed Eastern Zhou horizon.
events.uncertainty: The exact findspot and archaeological context are unrecorded; historical use as a weapon or dates of manufacture cannot be observed directly. The 2006 study is not the ancient use date. The makers are inferred from the finished object, and actual firing is not documented.

events.label: 500–301 BCE
events.statement: CB3 shaft: cast to rod shape, then decarburized to low-carbon iron.
events.uncertainty: Museum attribution lacks a recorded excavation context; process is inferred from microstructure.

events.label: by c. 301 BCE (museum attribution)
events.statement: A composite bronze-headed crossbow bolt with an iron shaft existed within the museum-attributed Eastern Zhou horizon; the shaft microstructure is interpreted as cast then decarburized.
events.uncertainty: The exact findspot and archaeological context are unrecorded; historical use as a weapon or dates of manufacture cannot be observed directly. The 2006 study is not the ancient use date. The makers are inferred from the finished object, and actual firing is not documented.

events.label: c. 1635
events.statement: Whipple Museum accession 0833 is a surviving Allen/Oughtred brass circular logarithmic instrument with fixed concentric scales and paired radial index arms.
events.uncertainty: Whipple dates accession 0833 approximately 1635; it is not Oxford 40,847 and the Oxford gift does not date this specimen or establish first conception.

events.statement: George Barkham gave the separately surviving Oxford example of the Allen/Oughtred circles of proportion to St John’s College; its inscription is dated 1635 and the museum says it reached Oxford almost directly after manufacture.
events.uncertainty: The 1919 catalogue records that movable parts apart from base and thumbscrews were then missing; their original configuration has not been established from the Oxford witness. The gift does not establish classroom operation, first use or sale. Oxford 40,847 and Whipple 0833 are different physical objects.

events.statement: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta chapter 18 treats positive, negative and zero quantities in addition, subtraction and multiplication; a multiplied quantity times zero gives zero.
events.uncertainty: Not an origin claim for zero notation. The division statements include zero divided by zero as zero; this is not a modern field-arithmetic rule. No direct transmission to a named Arabic text is established here.

events.label: Around the ninth century
events.statement: Pṛthūdaka’s commentary works through Brahmagupta’s algebraic chapter, which includes the zero and signed-number rules.
events.uncertainty: The commentator’s precise date, original manuscripts, and wider use of each rule are uncertain; this is commentary-based engagement, not proof of the rules’ first uptake.

events.label: by the 1202 composition
events.statement: Leonardo Pisano reports receiving instruction in calculation with the nine Indian figures while his father served the Pisan merchant community at Bugia.
events.uncertainty: This is autobiographical testimony preserved in the revised work. The teacher's identity, exact year, language and ethnic identity are not supplied and are not guessed.

events.label: By 1202
events.statement: Leonardo recounts being taught calculation using Indian figures in Bugia.
events.uncertainty: The instruction is not precisely dated; its teacher’s name, breadth of local practice, and exact start are unknown.

events.statement: Galileo's progressively improved convex-objective/concave-eyepiece telescopes, with selected or manufactured lenses adequate for his lunar and later planetary observations.
events.uncertainty: A sequence of instruments, not one unchanged telescope. Claimed thirty-power performance is not adopted as a measured specification of the discovery instrument.

events.label: November–December 1609
events.statement: Galileo used an improved telescope in a sustained program of observations and lunar drawings.
events.uncertainty: The exact telescope used for every lunar drawing is not separately identified; later Jupiter instruments need not be identical.

events.statement: Worked computational illustrations of Ibn al-Banna's rules, including 4043 + 2685 = 6728 with a zero place and explicit carrying between ranks.
events.uncertainty: The 2021 translation normalizes figures for reading; original manuscript glyph forms should be checked separately before drawing a paleographic lineage. Worked examples are not proof of population-wide adoption.

events.label: 18 July 1345 (Julian)
events.statement: The Medina manuscript copy of al-Hawārī’s commentary was completed on 18 July 1345 Julian.
events.uncertainty: The scribe’s exact understanding and readers’ use of the particular 4043 + 2685 example are not established; earlier transmission is possible. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

events.label: before 1301
events.statement: Condensed Book on the Operations of Arithmetic gives rules for known and unknown quantities, including place-aligned addition, without worked numerical examples.
events.uncertainty: No invention claim for the rules. Dating is a terminus before 1301; the wide interval encodes limited evidence rather than continuous development over the author's life.

events.label: Early 1305
events.statement: Ibn al-Bannāʾ taught his Condensed Book to students, including al-Hawārī, in early 1305.
events.uncertainty: This is an observed class, not proof that all students adopted all procedures or that it was first taught in 1305.

events.label: c. 825
events.statement: Arithmetic procedures using nine numeral signs and decimal places, with a small circle for an empty place, attributed to Indian reckoning in the later Latin textual tradition.
events.uncertainty: The Arabic original and original Arabic title are lost. Details are reconstructed through Latin redactions, not directly read from an Arabic ninth-century manuscript; no particular Sanskrit source is identified.

events.label: 13th-century copy
events.statement: A manuscript copy transmits al-Khwārizmī-derived procedures, transmitted through the Latin adaptation.
events.uncertainty: The Arabic original is lost and the Latin is mediated; the manuscript date is a scholarly range, not a proven first reception. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

events.label: 12th c.
events.statement: Latin reworking of al-Khwarizmi-derived arithmetic, preserving decimal positions, nine numeral signs and a small-circle placeholder; includes operational arithmetic rules.
events.uncertainty: Cambridge Ii.6.5 and New York HC 397/726 preserve differing revisions, not the lost first translation. Neither a named translator nor Toledo is asserted as settled.

events.label: 13th-century copy
events.statement: A manuscript copy transmits the Latin Dixit Algorizmi reworking.
events.uncertainty: The Arabic original is lost and the Latin is mediated; the manuscript date is a scholarly range, not a proven first reception. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

events.label: 12th c.
events.statement: A separate Latin arithmetic exposition expanding and arranging al-Khwarizmi-derived calculation methods, including operations on integers and fractions and square-root extraction.
events.uncertainty: The magister Iohannes named as author is not securely identified with John of Seville. The precise relation and order of Liber Alchorismi and Liber pulveris are not resolved here.

events.label: 13th-century manuscript
events.statement: The Oxford manuscript Selden supra 26 preserves an incomplete copy of the first part of Liber Alchorismi.
events.uncertainty: The text’s adaptation is often dated to the twelfth century, but the surviving copy does not show the first actual readership; it is incomplete. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established. The Oxford witness is incomplete; the particular presence of every integer, fraction and square-root procedure was not verified.

events.label: 1228 revision
events.statement: The revised Liber abaci teaches writing numbers with nine figures plus 0, decimal place values and explicit empty-place examples such as 209, alongside arithmetic procedures.
events.uncertainty: The opening heading recalls 1202, but surviving content must not automatically be assigned to that lost first version. No broad merchant adoption is inferred from the text's existence.

events.label: Late 13th to early 14th century (estimated)
events.statement: A Siena manuscript preserves the first page of the revised Liber abaci, including its numeral teaching.
events.uncertainty: Devlin says late 13th century; Germano extends the estimate into the early 14th century. The half-century endpoints are conventional estimates, not secure dating limits. Current Siena custody does not establish where it was copied; copying does not prove arithmetic use.

events.statement: Published logarithmic calculation and tables, in Napier's original normalization rather than modern base-10 form.
events.uncertainty: No universal priority asserted; independent logarithmic developments are outside the current scope.

events.label: 10 March 1615
events.statement: Briggs wrote that he was occupied with Napier’s logarithms after reading the published work.
events.uncertainty: The letter does not specify the exact first day Briggs began, nor does it establish general acceptance of every table. Teaching to students is described as subsequent, but is not independently dated by 10 March.

events.statement: The erasable-board arithmetic taken as the starting configuration in al-Uqlidisi's treatment: digits and intermediate results can be erased or shifted during calculation.
events.uncertainty: No preserved tenth-century board is claimed. This node dates the described practice in the book, not its first regional use.

events.label: By 952–953
events.statement: Al-Uqlīdisī associates the dust board with people earning a living by astrology in the streets.
events.uncertainty: The account survives through a later copy; the source does not establish that all such astrologers were in Damascus or that all used identical boards.

events.statement: Pen-and-paper calculation procedures avoiding the earlier erasure operation; one described multiplication combines Indian operand digits with abjad-written intermediate products.
events.uncertainty: The passage describes a method, not universal displacement of dust boards or invention of paper. Abjad and Indian signs coexisted; the book is not a simple replacement story.

events.label: July 1157 copy
events.statement: The surviving manuscript of the treatise containing pen-and-paper methods was copied in July 1157.
events.uncertainty: Copying is not proof that the method was widely adopted; the author states reasons for moving away from dust boards, and uptake appears slow. The surviving witness supports access by its copyist; the copyist’s location and practical execution are not established.

events.label: c. 1775–76
events.statement: Wilkinson's large-cylinder machining: a stationary cylinder secured on its bed and a rotating boring bar supported beyond both ends, with the cutter fed along the bar.
events.uncertainty: The 1775–76 dating attaches securely to the output/supply episode; association with the exact reconstructed machine is less secure. Gilpin's original plan was not independently inspected. Museum loading details, works-founding date and universal priority claims are excluded.

events.label: by 1776-03-11
events.statement: A historian reconstructs this through-bar method for large early Watt cylinders; its association with the Bloomfield cylinder by March 1776 is a contextual inference.
events.uncertainty: The Gilpin drawing is later and no original machining log establishes that the Bloomfield cylinder used this exact arrangement or that all features already existed by 1776.

events.label: by 11 March 1776
events.statement: Boulton & Watt's single-acting mine-pumping engine at Bloomfield, with a 50-inch cylinder ordered from Wilkinson in June 1775.
events.uncertainty: The original Gazette issue and original cylinder order were not independently inspected; the 1868 newspaper transcription was inspected. This does not establish a first commercial offer or universal priority.

events.statement: Watt's surviving second cylinder-and-separate-condenser model; condensation occurs outside the working cylinder.
events.uncertainty: Formerly misidentified as the first model. The museum describes alterations and probable sealing difficulties; reliable prolonged operation is not claimed.

events.label: by 11 March 1776
events.statement: A separate-condenser Watt engine was set to work pumping at Bloomfield Colliery in the presence of the colliery proprietors and other witnesses by 11 March 1776.
events.uncertainty: This concerns the deployed Bloomfield engine, not operation of the surviving second model. The original newspaper issue was not separately inspected; Langford’s 1868 printed transcription was inspected. No first commercial offer or universal uptake is asserted.

events.statement: Watt describes alternating steam admission and condensation above and below the piston, transmitting both push and pull through rack-and-sector or other connections.
events.uncertainty: A patent describes claimed arrangements; it does not alone establish operation or the stated doubling of actual output.

events.statement: A double-acting rack-and-sector engine worked a corn mill at Soho in 1783.
events.uncertainty: The source dates actual operation to 1783 but disagrees on the month; this does not establish a public offer or use of every alternative in the specification.

events.label: 1785 drawing
events.statement: Boulton & Watt elevation of the Robinson cotton mill showing an 11-horsepower sun-and-planet engine with 17½-inch cylinder and four-foot stroke, alongside evidence of the earlier waterwheel.
events.uncertainty: The catalogue supplies the installation interpretation and dimensions; the original-resolution drawing was not inspected for this claim. No cotton-industry priority claim or exact operating start is adopted.

events.label: by 1786
events.statement: A Boulton & Watt sun-and-planet engine powered the Robinson cotton mill at Papplewick by 1786.
events.uncertainty: Historic England dates steam-powered cotton spinning at Papplewick to 1786; Gedling dates the Robinson factory’s steam power to 1785. The archive interprets the drawing and dimensions; the drawing as built was not independently verified. No precise commissioning day or global priority is asserted.

events.label: 1847 publication
events.statement: Published measurements of saturated-steam pressure and latent heat per unit mass, undertaken for steam-engine calculations; Thomson describes the published range as 0–230 °C and the missing density information needed for his calculations.
events.uncertainty: The recipient’s contemporary account and bibliographic record were inspected; Regnault’s underlying experimental volume was not retrieved (Gallica 403). No claim of auditing its apparatus or tables.

events.label: by October 1848
events.statement: By the October 1848 publication, Thomson had used Regnault’s steam data when calculating a comparison for his thermometric scale.
events.uncertainty: The underlying Regnault tables were not audited. The publication bounds Thomson’s actual use but does not date it exactly or establish market distribution or universal adoption.

events.statement: Watt's fifth patented method converts reciprocating engine motion into continuous shaft rotation with sun-and-planet gearing; the specification also describes an internal-tooth variant.
events.uncertainty: The primary specification was read in a web transcription of a scholarly documentary edition. Its OCR errors and intermediate hosting are recorded; invention priority between Watt and Murdock is not asserted.

events.statement: A Soho double-acting engine used the internal sun-and-planet gearing included in Watt’s 1781 patent to drive a corn mill.
events.uncertainty: The operating month is disputed. This shows use of the internal variant, not market availability of all five mechanisms in the specification.

events.statement: The same Soho double-reciprocating engine was subsequently applied to lathes and drills in the engine shops; Southern called it the boring engine.
events.uncertainty: The conversion year, individual tools, and products made with them are not identified. No arrow back to the earlier Wilkinson machine is asserted.

events.statement: An 18-inch-cylinder, double-acting rotative engine using rack-and-sector connection and internal sun-and-planet gear, initially driving a corn mill.
events.uncertainty: Item-level catalogue inspected, not all drawings or diary leaves. The catalogue notes conflicting stroke lengths and first-operation records; no precise stroke or month is asserted.

events.statement: The engine was initially used to drive a corn mill at Soho in 1783.
events.uncertainty: Sources cited by the archive disagree on the month and stroke; no customer sale or first market offer is inferred.

events.label: by 24 April 1775 or 1776; letter year disputed
events.statement: An approximately 18-inch replacement cylinder machined by John Wilkinson and supplied for Watt's experimental engine at Soho.
events.uncertainty: The actual machine used for this small cylinder is not securely identified. Andrew proposes a rotating-workpiece cannon-boring machine as a likelihood; that conjecture is not adopted as fact. The 1854 edition has conflicting 1775 and 1776 letter dates; Andrew follows 1775. The original manuscript has not been inspected, so a suspected printing error is not resolved here.

events.statement: Muirhead’s published letter disclosed the supplied cylinder; Andrew attributes the supply to Wilkinson.
events.uncertainty: No sale or earlier public disclosure of this exact small cylinder was established. The published heading prints 1776, the contents print 1775, and the underlying original letter was not examined.

events.label: 16–22 July 1969
events.statement: The crew left the damaged Ra at sea and reached Barbados aboard Shenandoah; the 1969 voyage in Ra was abandoned.
events.uncertainty: First departure and final decision may not be the same moment. The contemporaneous interview says the later fate of Ra was then unknown; this event applies only to Ra and that voyage.

events.label: 25 May 1969
events.statement: Ra departed Safi on the expedition’s experimental Atlantic voyage.
events.uncertainty: A voyage beginning is not evidence of historical pre-Columbian contact and does not imply the crossing succeeded.

events.statement: The papyrus vessel Ra was built in 1969 for the expedition.
events.uncertainty: Construction month and day are not specified; this is not a claim about the invention of reed boats. The museum page has conflicting Giza prose and a Safi caption; the contemporary Salén-Nytt account independently corroborates Giza.

events.statement: Zeiss listed the 1/18 homogeneous-immersion objective at 400 marks without a correction mount and described the series as stocked in fixed mounts.
events.uncertainty: This is an observed priced offering, not proof of the first-ever offer. Corrected-mount price was 450 marks and made on request.

events.label: Between the 1885 and 1889 catalogues
events.statement: By its 1889 catalogue, Zeiss said it no longer supplied the former 1/18 homogeneous-immersion objective.
events.uncertainty: Exact withdrawal date is not given. Does not establish the end of existing owners use, other firms products, or all achromatic objectives.

events.label: Third century CE (traditional 263 dating)
events.statement: Liu Hui studied and wrote a sustained commentary on the Nine Chapters.
events.uncertainty: The exact compilation date and the traditional year 263 for his undated commentary are debated; no first readership is claimed.

events.label: Third century CE (traditional 263 dating)
events.statement: Liu Hui interpreted and extended the chapter 8 procedures for linear systems.
events.uncertainty: The commentary and received text are composite historical witnesses; modern matrix terminology is descriptive, not a claim of identical formalism or invention date.

events.statement: Li Chunfeng’s group produced a subcommentary on the base text and Liu Hui’s commentary, presented to the throne in 656.
events.uncertainty: The 656 work is a group effort; the surviving textual layers can blur, and this does not establish a first readership for Liu’s commentary.

events.statement: The group supervised by Li Chunfeng presented its subcommentary to the Tang throne.
events.uncertainty: The record identifies submission to the throne, but does not show that a particular ruler or official read or endorsed it, or prove dissemination beyond the court. Portions of received commentary layers may be blurred.

events.statement: The Imperial Library printed an edition of the Nine Chapters with the two traditional commentaries in 1084.
events.uncertainty: Printing does not prove a specific person read this edition or that it was the first circulation; the earliest extant reprint is later.

events.label: Approximately 1010 CE
events.statement: Karpinski identifies al-Karajī’s al-Fakhrī as reusing algebraic problems and solutions from Abū Kāmil’s treatise.
events.uncertainty: Karpinski’s attribution rests on a historian’s comparison: al-Karajī did not name Abū Kāmil, and the original al-Fakhrī and its Arabic manuscript witnesses were not independently examined for this record. The estimated composition around 1010 is approximate; a modern presentation lists alternative death estimates around 1019 and 1029. None establishes an exact composition day, publication date, or first reception.

events.label: By 1184
events.statement: Al-Qurashī wrote an algebraic commentary on Abū Kāmil’s treatise.
events.uncertainty: The commentary itself has not been recovered; Ibn Khaldūn and later fragments supply indirect testimony. The original book is not the same work as Ibn al-Bannāʾ’s arithmetic.

events.label: By 1407 (identity and death-date uncertain)
events.statement: Ibn Zakariyā’s book preserves fragments of al-Qurashī’s algebra commentary.
events.uncertainty: Djebbar’s 2013 account gives the commentator’s death as 1404, while his 2018 account gives 1407 for Ibn Zakariyā of Granada; identifying the two references is an inference pending direct comparison of the underlying manuscript. The earlier commentary survives only indirectly; neither first circulation nor a direct influence on Ibn al-Bannāʾ is established.

events.label: 19th–17th century BCE (Old Babylonian)
events.statement: A student scribe produced a signed multiplication-table school tablet.
events.uncertainty: The catalogue marks Nippur as uncertain; the teacher, classroom and exact year are not established.

events.label: 19th–17th century BCE (Old Babylonian)
events.statement: A scribe wrote a square diagram with a numerical diagonal and an approximation to the square root of two.
events.uncertainty: Whether the scribe calculated the numbers independently or copied a worked example is not established; southern Mesopotamian origin is tentative.

events.label: About 1650–1550 BCE (different scholarly estimates)
events.statement: Aḥmose copied a mathematical text that includes arithmetic and geometric problems.
events.uncertainty: The British Museum estimates about 1550 BCE, while Chace’s older edition gives about 1650 BCE; the competing estimates and approximate range do not establish an exact copying year. The particular copied exemplar is lost; the scribe’s understanding and contemporary readership are not demonstrated.

events.statement: A Gwalior inscription records garden dimensions and a daily flower provision using decimal numerals with zero marks.
events.uncertainty: This is a dated historical use of a placeholder, not a claim that this was the earliest zero or evidence of Brahmagupta’s distinct arithmetic rules.

events.label: By approximately the first half of the second century CE
events.statement: Nicomachus described the numerical common-measure method in his Introduction to Arithmetic.
events.uncertainty: The textual witness and its composition date are transmitted through later editions. This occurrence is an earlier scholarly description, not proof of first use or dissemination of this passage to a specific audience.

events.label: By approximately 325 CE
events.statement: Iamblichus explained the common-measure method in his scholarly treatment of Nicomachus, including an odd-number example.
events.uncertainty: The sources do not establish when or where this numerical procedure was first used, that Nicomachus or Iamblichus read Euclid VII.2 directly, or that either consulted the later 888 Bodleian manuscript. Iamblichus’s life dates and the chronology of his commentary are approximate; his explicit example concerns two odd numbers.

events.statement: Stephen copied a manuscript of the Elements containing the Book VII greatest-common-measure proposition.
events.uncertainty: The manuscript was written for Arethas, but his receipt or independent calculation is not established here; the event is not the invention date.

events.label: By 1408
events.statement: Al-ʿUqbānī used al-Qurashī’s fraction method in his commentary on al-Hūfī by the end of his life in 1408.
events.uncertainty: Both accounts are by Ahmed Djebbar: his later article describes extensive teaching and application, while the earlier account says most legal practitioners continued an older method. Their geographic coverage and precise denominators are not established; the claims do not independently corroborate one another, and neither identifies a first use.

events.label: by c. 350 CE (Meroitic use inferred)
events.statement: The Great Hafir stored local water used in the Musawwarat religious-site system.
events.uncertainty: The Great Hafir’s construction is radiocarbon-constrained to the 6th–4th centuries BCE; neither its original commissioning nor the ducts’ precise age is individually dated. The 350 CE endpoint is only a broad Meroitic contextual estimate, not a hard archaeological cutoff.

events.label: by c. 350 CE (inferred)
events.statement: The excavated inlet and earthworks are interpreted as having directed runoff into the Great Hafir reservoir.
events.uncertainty: The Great Hafir’s construction is radiocarbon-constrained to the 6th–4th centuries BCE; neither its original commissioning nor the ducts’ precise age is individually dated. The 350 CE endpoint is only a broad Meroitic contextual estimate, not a hard archaeological cutoff.

events.label: by c. 350 CE (inferred)
events.statement: A duct from the Great Hafir is interpreted as supplying the Great Enclosure.
events.uncertainty: The Great Hafir’s construction is radiocarbon-constrained to the 6th–4th centuries BCE; neither its original commissioning nor the ducts’ precise age is individually dated. The 350 CE endpoint is only a broad Meroitic contextual estimate, not a hard archaeological cutoff.

events.label: by c. 900 CE
events.statement: UNESCO describes cooperative subak water management with ninth-century roots.
events.uncertainty: UNESCO’s broad summary does not date each existing temple, channel, rule or local group to the ninth century; this is not proof of uniform or uninterrupted institutions.

events.label: by c. 1000 CE
events.statement: A spring dam at Tirta Empul was repaired in the tenth-century inscription’s account.
events.uncertainty: The inscription is read through a modern academic study; exact year conversions and the earlier construction date are uncertain. Repair indicates a pre-existing configuration but does not show continuous use.

events.label: by c. 1000 CE
events.statement: The inscription describes use of the spring’s water for irrigation.
events.uncertainty: The 2023 study interprets the inscription rather than providing an independently inspected translation here; exact fields, first-use year, and continuity with named modern subaks remain unestablished.

events.label: by the end of the 15th century
events.statement: The connected Inka road system supported state movement and communications by the fifteenth-century expansion.
events.uncertainty: The network was assembled over time from routes with different ages; the bound does not assign a date to each surviving segment or prove free public access.

events.label: by 1554 (retrospective manuscript account)
events.statement: Named state messengers operated a relay along Inka roads, as reconstructed from early colonial descriptions.
events.uncertainty: Cieza’s account is retrospective and mediated through a later translation; use is dated no later than the author’s 1554 death, not to its nineteenth-century publication. Exact first use, universal spacing and identification of any specific surviving site remain uncertain.

events.label: by 1554 (retrospective manuscript account)
events.statement: Small roadside posts housed replacement messengers for the documented relay system.
events.uncertainty: Cieza’s account is retrospective and mediated through a later translation; use is dated no later than the author’s 1554 death, not to its nineteenth-century publication. Exact first use, universal spacing and identification of any specific surviving site remain uncertain.

events.statement: In 1533 Inka accountants recorded supplies withdrawn from a storehouse using knotted cords.
events.uncertainty: This is one reported administrative use during the Spanish occupation, not the origin of khipu, a decoding of the specific string values or evidence that these particular cords traveled by chaski.

events.label: by c. 1600 CE (inferred)
events.statement: The Keawanui enclosed pond was operated in the local managed-fishery setting.
events.uncertainty: Construction is approximate and initial use is inferred; chiefly control and unequal access are not generalized into common ownership. Later restoration is separate.

events.label: probably within a decade of construction
events.statement: Field observations and hydrological modeling led the authors to infer probable early overtopping and failure of the embankment.
events.uncertainty: The date, failure sequence and wider consequences are hypotheses, not an eyewitness account or an exact date of total abandonment.

events.label: by c. 950 CE (inferred)
events.statement: The embankment is interpreted as storing river water and providing a crest route linking Koh Ker with the highway before the hypothesized breach.
events.uncertainty: Water storage and crest-route function are archaeological interpretations; named users, unrestricted access, complete commissioning and individual operating dates are not proved. Probable construction and early failure are model-based estimates.

events.label: by c. 950 CE (inferred)
events.statement: The surviving main spillway and chute are interpreted as having carried reservoir outflow; erosion and displaced laterite indicate water passage, probably including destructive flows.
events.uncertainty: The paper interprets flow from erosion, displaced blocks and hydraulic modeling; the separate timing, routine service and hydraulic performance of each outlet are uncertain. Failure may have occurred soon after construction and exact named operators are unknown.

events.label: by c. 900 BCE
events.statement: Northern Chinese foundries cast bronze using clay models, section molds and cores.
events.uncertainty: The museum presents a broad retrospective historical interval; this does not date the first mold use, each artifact, exchange or global priority.

events.label: by c. 1301 BCE
events.statement: A cast-glass heart amulet was made for the Egyptian funerary-amulet tradition.
events.uncertainty: The surviving object and general funerary function do not document which individual wore this artifact, its exact deposition or a sale.

events.label: by c. 1050 BCE (contextual)
events.statement: A broken white pottery jar and lid were placed in the Shang burial at Hsiao-t’un tomb M331.
events.uncertainty: The institute interprets the jar as broken before burial; the reason for breakage and any prior use are unknown. M331 dating is contested, so the mid-eleventh-century BCE terminus is a broad approximate Yinxu context, not a measured deposition date. No stoneware firing temperature is asserted for this jar.

events.label: by c. 50 CE
events.statement: The Ennion workshop made a surviving multipart mold-blown glass jug.
events.uncertainty: The attribution and dating are museum judgments; the exact workshop location, purchaser and commissioning date remain uncertain.

events.label: by c. 500 CE
events.statement: Maya artists used the indigo–palygorskite pigment in painted art by the late fifth century.
events.uncertainty: The source is a later synthesis citing earlier work, not a newly dated first pigment sample; c. 500 is an approximate contextual bound, and the material was used in distinct Mesoamerican communities.

events.label: by c. 700 CE
events.statement: Mold-blown souvenir bottles were sold to pilgrims in the sixth–seventh-century Holy Land.
events.uncertainty: The cited museum gives no first-sale day, individual buyer record or proof this particular surviving vessel was sold.

events.label: by c. 850 CE
events.statement: Some Xing-attributed whiteware vessels were carried among the ship’s cargo.
events.uncertainty: The cargo includes pieces from several kiln groups; individual attributions, destination and sale are not established, and the ship did not reach its planned destination.

events.label: by c. 850 CE
events.statement: Three Gongxian blue-and-white dishes were included in the ship’s merchant cargo.
events.uncertainty: The precise kiln and decoration sequence remain scholarly interpretations; shipment does not establish an eventual sale or receiver.

events.label: by 1891
events.statement: Pittsburgh Reduction scaled up production of aluminum ingots and fabricated products at New Kensington.
events.uncertainty: Corporate retrospective; the exact first heat, customer transactions, and specific product provenance are not established by this timeline.

events.statement: Pittsburgh Reduction entered the household cookware market with aluminum teakettles.
events.uncertainty: The historical corporate timeline does not identify a first customer or prove the first aluminum cookware in every market.

events.statement: The Wright Flyer flew in 1903 with an engine crankcase/block cast from aluminum supplied by Pittsburgh Reduction.
events.uncertainty: This is a supplier’s retrospective account. The source does not identify which aluminum works produced the specific metal or prove any global first use in engines.

events.label: by 15 March 1935
events.statement: By 15 March 1935 a contemporary report identified the new Bakelite-cased Ekco AD36 and quoted a retail price.
events.uncertainty: The priced contemporary receiver report supports the local market offer, not a confirmed sale, universal shop stock or the first commercial offer. Full PDF bytes were unavailable; the retained excerpt consists of attributed verbatim OCR lines.

events.label: by April 1935
events.statement: The Bakelite-cased Ekco AD36 had appeared in shop windows with a published price by April 1935.
events.uncertainty: The cached text is a brief OCR excerpt of a contemporary review; original PDF bytes could not be retained. This is not a claim that the AD36 was the first Bakelite product or that every shop stocked it.

events.label: by 24 February 1938
events.statement: By the named product’s first reported sale, Weco had incorporated DuPont nylon filament as its toothbrush bristles.
events.uncertainty: The museum retrospective supports use in this named consumer product, not the first bulk nylon transaction or every later application. Bristles were incorporated before or by the product sale; the first use in manufacture is not separately dated. The source identifies Weco as a Chicago company but does not locate manufacture or a transaction.

events.label: 24 February 1938
events.statement: Weco began selling the Dr West’s Miracle-Tuft nylon-bristle toothbrush.
events.uncertainty: The museum retrospective is not a surviving sales invoice, and the claim is scoped to this toothbrush rather than all nylon products. The source identifies Weco as a Chicago company but does not locate manufacture or a transaction.

events.label: by 749 CE, archaeological horizon
events.statement: Multiple parallel cuts and a water-race installation indicate local productive stone sawing in the dated historical horizon.
events.uncertainty: The mechanism and precise operating dates are reconstructed, and the 749 date is a broad upper limit rather than the start of use.

events.label: by c. 700 CE
events.statement: Partly cut in-situ blocks and the workshop water channel indicate a local productive sawing application.
events.uncertainty: Crank, wheel support and blade-frame details are competing modern reconstructions; no direct ancestry from Hierapolis or Gerasa is established.

events.label: 1769 completion
events.statement: Kendall completed K1, a copy of H4, in 1769.
events.uncertainty: Completion is not a date of first use or commercial offer.

events.label: by 1775
events.statement: The museum identifies the K1 watch as used to determine longitude during the 1772–1775 voyage.
events.uncertainty: The source does not establish the first day it was used or general availability of affordable chronometers.

events.label: by the 1773 voyage
events.statement: The Board issued the simplified K2 watch to Phipps for an actual naval voyage.
events.uncertainty: Issue to the expedition does not establish that a particular observation was made, the watch’s performance, fleet-wide availability or any sale.

events.label: by 7 August 1781
events.statement: The 1778 Shadwell engine used expansive working; a later dated report of its broken piston rod supports contextual operation by August 1781.
events.uncertainty: The archive record is a modern summary of correspondence, not the original letter; no exact first operating day is established.

events.label: by c. 1779
events.statement: The museum identifies Old Bess as the water-returning mill engine; Watt’s quoted memoir places the larger replacement around 1778–1779.
events.uncertainty: The museum’s 1777 attribution conflicts with the quoted 1778–1779 replacement chronology; exact commissioning and machine alterations are unresolved.

events.label: by June 1796
events.statement: The Newcomen mine pump was installed for dewatering, and a 1796 colliery fuel ledger is interpreted as evidence of its operation by June 1796.
events.uncertainty: Installation is described as 1795 or 1796 by different Historic England records. The 1796 ledger does not identify the engine by type; Barnsley Museums treats the attribution as an assumption. A first pumping day is not established.

events.label: by 1831
events.statement: The surviving lathe was used by Maudslay to make accurate screw threads; the museum dates the machine to around 1800.
events.uncertainty: Exact individual shop orders, first use and original change gears are not documented by this source; the death-year bound is inferential.

events.label: 1803 initial operation
events.statement: The Navy’s Portsmouth block-making machinery was operating by 1803 with steam power and sequential specialist machinery.
events.uncertainty: One installed set operated by 1803; this is not a claim the whole system was complete then or the first mechanized production worldwide.

events.label: by March 1805
events.statement: The original coaking machine was installed in the Navy’s Portsmouth block mill and belonged to its operating sequence.
events.uncertainty: A precise first operation date for this individual machine is not reported; its relationship to the operating sequence is a contextual inference.

events.statement: The railway used electric telegraph messages for the winding engines.
events.uncertainty: Specific needle count and start month not identified.

events.statement: The Post Office opened the Washington–Baltimore line for paid public use.
events.uncertainty: Do not infer first telegraph service worldwide, first transaction or profitability.

events.statement: Public use began and people used telegraph offices.
events.uncertainty: Abstract only; individual class, regional and price barriers remain unassessed.

events.statement: Queen Victoria’s message to U.S. President James Buchanan was sent across the 1858 cable on 16 August.
events.uncertainty: The cable failed within weeks; the later business message is not assumed to prove a paid public tariff or a continuing service.

events.statement: The U.S. legation in Paris received a transatlantic cable message from Cyrus Field in Newfoundland.
events.uncertainty: This receipt does not establish the first customer message or general public tariffs.

events.label: by August 1866
events.statement: By August 1866, Scientific American reported that its London correspondent’s transatlantic message had incurred a cable charge under a published schedule.
events.uncertainty: The cited 2020 publisher republication attributes the account to August 1866, but the original issue was not independently inspected and the exact message date, payment settlement, first sale and global tariffs are not established.

events.statement: NTT dates telegraph service in Tokyo and Yokohama to 1870.
events.uncertainty: Only the year is used; calendar conversion and exact public tariff remain unassessed.

events.label: by 1878-01-28
events.statement: Coy’s New Haven exchange was providing subscriber service by 28 January 1878; the 1907 account reports earlier service on 21 January.
events.uncertainty: Accounts differ on the first service date and subscriber count: NPS reports 21 subscribers with the 28 January start, while De Land reports approximately 30 for initial service on 21 January and a 28 January formal opening. The record establishes availability by 28 January, not an undisputed first day or headcount.

events.statement: Pearl Street began commercial central electricity service.
events.uncertainty: Do not infer universal city coverage, adoption elsewhere, or a first date for electricity sales.

events.statement: On 25 August the long-distance line supplied around 900 exhibition lamps.
events.uncertainty: Exhibition supply is not evidence of paid municipal service or worldwide adoption. The waterfall’s 25 August operation is not asserted.

events.statement: Hydroelectric power was delivered under contract from Niagara Falls to the Buffalo Railway Company just after midnight on 16 November 1896.
events.uncertainty: The report describes an opening test and contracted delivery; uninterrupted subsequent operation, wider public tariffs, generating-phase details and the first commercial sale remain separate questions.
